subject: bio
title: Nucleic Acids and Protein Synthesis
subtitle: DNA structure, replication, transcription and translation.
concept: DNA is a double helix of antiparallel polynucleotide strands held together by complementary base pairing (A–T, G–C).
DNA replication is semi-conservative: each new molecule contains one original and one new strand, confirmed by Meselson and Stahl.
Protein synthesis: transcription (DNA → mRNA in nucleus) then translation (mRNA → protein at ribosomes).

notes.heading: DNA Structure
items: DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel polynucleotide strands. Each nucleotide consists of a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group, and one of four nitrogenous bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G) or cytosine (C).

Complementary base pairing: A pairs with T via 2 hydrogen bonds; G pairs with C via 3 hydrogen bonds. The two strands are antiparallel — one runs 5'→3', the other 3'→5'. Adjacent nucleotides within a strand are linked by covalent phosphodiester bonds.

notes.heading: DNA Replication (Semi-Conservative)
items: Helicase unwinds the double helix and breaks the hydrogen bonds between base pairs, separating the two strands. Each strand then serves as a template.

DNA polymerase adds free nucleotides complementary to the template strand, building a new strand in the 5'→3' direction only. The leading strand is synthesised continuously; the lagging strand is built in short Okazaki fragments.

DNA ligase joins the Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand. The result is two identical double-stranded DNA molecules, each containing one original strand and one new strand — hence semi-conservative.
Meselson and Stahl proved semi-conservative replication using ¹⁵N and ¹⁴N isotopes in caesium chloride density gradient centrifugation.

notes.heading: Transcription
items: RNA polymerase binds to the promoter region and unwinds a section of DNA. It reads the template (antisense) strand 3'→5' and synthesises a complementary mRNA strand 5'→3'.
RNA uses uracil (U) instead of thymine — so where the template has A, the mRNA has U. The coding (sense) strand has the same sequence as the mRNA (with U replacing T).

In eukaryotes, the initial pre-mRNA is processed: introns (non-coding sequences) are spliced out, exons are joined, and a 5' methylguanosine cap and poly-A tail are added — protecting the mRNA and aiding ribosome binding.

notes.heading: Translation
items: The mature mRNA leaves the nucleus through nuclear pores and attaches to a ribosome (in the cytoplasm or on the RER). Each codon (three consecutive bases) on the mRNA specifies one amino acid.
tRNA molecules carry specific amino acids to the ribosome. The anticodon on each tRNA is complementary to the mRNA codon. AUG is the start codon (methionine); UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons.

The ribosome moves along the mRNA; peptide bonds form between successive amino acids as tRNA molecules deliver them. The growing polypeptide chain is released when a stop codon is reached, then folds into its tertiary shape.

definitions.body: Each new DNA molecule consists of one original (parental) strand and one newly synthesised strand.
A sequence of three bases on mRNA that codes for a specific amino acid (or start/stop signal).
A sequence of three bases on tRNA that is complementary to a specific mRNA codon.
The process of synthesising mRNA from a DNA template in the nucleus.
The process of synthesising a polypeptide from the information encoded in mRNA, occurring at ribosomes.

workedExamples.q: A DNA template strand reads 3'–TAC GGA CTT–5'. Write the mRNA sequence and the amino acids coded (use AUG = Met, CCU = Pro, GAA = Glu).

steps.text: Template 3'–TAC GGA CTT–5' → mRNA 5'–AUG CCU GAA–3'
AUG = Met; CCU = Pro; GAA = Glu

mistakes: Confusing the template strand (used for transcription) with the coding strand (same sequence as mRNA but with T not U).
Forgetting that mRNA contains uracil (U) not thymine (T).
Describing replication as 'conservative' (both strands are new) — it is semi-conservative.
tips: Meselson & Stahl: used ¹⁵N (heavy) and ¹⁴N (light) nitrogen in CsCl density gradient centrifugation to prove semi-conservative replication.
tRNA anticodon is complementary AND antiparallel to mRNA codon — check your base pairing carefully.
Remember: helicase unwinds; DNA polymerase builds; ligase joins.

flashcards.q: What base pairing rules apply in DNA?
flashcards.a: A pairs with T (2 H-bonds); G pairs with C (3 H-bonds). Antiparallel strands.
Each daughter DNA molecule contains one original strand and one newly synthesised strand.
Unwinds the DNA double helix by breaking hydrogen bonds between base pairs.

flashcards.q: What is the start codon and what amino acid does it code for?
What is the role of tRNA in translation?
flashcards.a: Carries a specific amino acid to the ribosome; its anticodon base-pairs with the complementary codon on mRNA.

flashcards.q: In which direction does DNA polymerase synthesise DNA?
flashcards.a: 5' to 3' only — new nucleotides are added to the 3' end of the growing strand.

questions.q: Which enzyme joins Okazaki fragments during DNA replication?
questions.exp: DNA ligase seals the gaps between Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand.

questions.q: A DNA strand reads 3'-ATCGTA-5'. What is the mRNA sequence?
questions.exp: Complementary RNA: A→U, T→A, C→G, G→C: 5'-UAGCAU-3'

questions.q: What is the role of RNA polymerase in transcription?
questions.exp: RNA polymerase synthesises mRNA by reading the template strand 3'→5' and building the RNA 5'→3'.

questions.q: How many hydrogen bonds hold a G–C base pair together?
questions.exp: G–C pairs have 3 hydrogen bonds; A–T pairs have 2.
Translation occurs at ribosomes — free in the cytoplasm or on the rough ER.
